items.body: Our third iteration of the " Sculpting Silence " series, brings us to France, for a trio with Alexandra Grimal on saxophones, voice, harmonium, nōkan, shakuhachi, Naoto Yamagishi on percussions and Alexandre Saada on piano and harmonium. The title, Marée Basse , is French for “low tide”: the moment when the sea withdraws, leaving behind a wide, empty stretch of beach scattered with shells, tiny creatures, and fragments the waves have carried ashore. The music evokes much the same landscape. It takes this open space for granted, allowing the notes of saxophone, piano, and percussion to appear sparsely, sometimes only for brief moments before disappearing again. All three musicians are minimalists, deeply attentive to the overall sound yet reluctant to impose themselves upon it, as though the tones themselves should determine whether, and when, they wish to interact. Every sound feels tender and fragile, unobtrusive and gentle—and often completely absent. Silence is not merely the space between the notes; it is an essential part of the music itself. This is particularly striking in the thirty-minute second track, where, roughly halfway through, there is almost a full minute of near silence, with only faint crackling sounds barely audible in the background. When the music gradually returns, the instrumentation has subtly shifted: the harmonium introduces a handful of sustained tones, joined by Grimal's wordless singing, equally elongated and sensitive. Towards the end of the piece, the sound becomes fuller and more agitated, as though a sudden gust of wind were stirring the waves and awakening the distant cries of seagulls. Once again, silence plays an essential role in this music, much as it does in Japanese art, which has fascinated Grimaldi in recent years. Here, absence is not a lack but a presence of its own—a space in which the smallest sounds can emerge, linger for a moment, and then quietly disappear. Enjoy! Listen and download from Bandcamp . items.body:
Eight years is a long time to wait, but Rachael Yamagata made her return to Singapore feel remarkably familiar.

Taking over Foo Chow Hall on 16 September, her Starlit Alchemy Tour marked her first show here since 2018, her 10th Singapore performance, and the tour’s only Southeast Asia stop. Early in the night, Yamagata spoke warmly about her history with the country and thanked Bandwagon for bringing her back — a fitting sentiment for an artist whose relationship with Singapore audiences has been built across numerous visits, long meet-and-greets, and years of songs that fans have carried with them.

The show itself embodied what makes Yamagata such a compelling live performer: enormous emotional weight without ever becoming oppressively solemn. There was tenderness and vulnerability, certainly, but also plenty of humour, stories, and an easy rapport with the room.

Opening with ‘Heaven Help’ and ‘Empty Houses’, Yamagata moved through a set that brought different eras of her catalogue into conversation. ‘Meet Me By the Water’ and ‘Saturday Morning’ appeared alongside ‘Break Apart’ and ‘Backwards’, before ‘Elephants’, ‘Over and Over’, ‘Dealbreaker’, ‘Sunday Afternoon’, and ‘You Won’t Let Me’ traced the emotional terrain she has explored across more than two decades of songwriting.

One of the night’s standout moments came with ‘Be Be Your Love’. Rather than its familiar piano-driven form, Yamagata presented the Happenstance favourite through a guitar-led arrangement that lost none of the original’s emotional force.

She dedicated it to opening act Charlie Lim, before jokingly protesting when Lim revealed that he had first heard the song when he was 15 — an admission that prompted Yamagata to playfully confront the passage of time.

The joke soon gave way to something more reflective. Yamagata acknowledged ‘Be Be Your Love’ as the breakthrough that helped open the doors to record deals and touring, making its return here feel especially poignant more than two decades on.

Lim, who recently returned with his third studio album DAYDREAM, was an inspired choice to open the evening, with his own emotionally direct, genre-fluid songwriting sharing natural ground with Yamagata’s. He later joined her for ‘Duet’, turning one of her best-loved collaborations into a distinctly Singaporean moment.

Then came an even more unexpected full-circle encounter.

Singaporean singer-songwriter, fitness personality, and content creator Tyen Rasif joined Yamagata for ‘I Wish You Love’. But Rasif’s connection with Yamagata did not begin backstage that evening.

Around 14 years ago, Rasif attended one of Yamagata’s Singapore concerts as a fan. Instead of joining the lengthy post-show meet-and-greet queue, she and her then-boyfriend happened to strike up a conversation with a stranger nearby. He turned out to be Yamagata’s producer, and after learning that the pair were aspiring singer-songwriters, invited them along for supper.

Yamagata was there — and the night eventually ended with them jamming together by the side of the road at around 5 AM.

14 later, Rasif was no longer singing with one of her musical heroes on a roadside. She was sharing a stage with her at Foo Chow Hall.

That full-circle moment captured much of what made Yamagata’s Singapore return so affecting. There were songs about loss and longing, but the night itself was filled with connection — between artist and audience, between old songs and new ones, and between musicians whose paths had crossed years earlier in very different circumstances.

Presented by Bandwagon Live in partnership with The Rock Promotions, MAILIVE, and MAISEAT, the concert ultimately showed why Yamagata’s relationship with Singapore has endured across 10 performances. She may have been away since 2018, but once the songs started, the distance did not feel quite so long.

items.body:
25 editions in, Baybeats 2026 proved that there is still plenty of room for discovery at Singapore's longest-running alternative music festival. Across 3 – 6 September, 48 acts filled Esplanade with everything from crushing experimental rock and abrasive post-punk to homegrown hip-hop and Thai roots reggae. It was diverse, unpredictable and, most importantly, a whole lot of fun. Here are five sets that stayed with us.

Boris

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by borisheavyrocks (@borisdronevil)

Few bands can make sheer volume feel as nuanced as Boris. The Japanese experimental rock veterans shifted through sludge, drone, noise, psychedelia and shoegaze with an almost elemental force, building enormous walls of sound before pulling them back into quieter, more hypnotic passages. Heavy without ever becoming one-dimensional, their set was a masterclass in how distortion, dynamics and atmosphere can work together to completely swallow a room.

DAVID BORING

Credit: danspixelgraphy, courtesy of Esplanade – Theatres on the Bay

There was something almost hypnotic about DAVID BORING, even at their most confrontational. The Hong Kong outfit constantly alternated between danceable, propulsive grooves and sudden bursts of abrasive post-punk noise, creating a tension between release and unease that kept the room locked in. That push and pull between raw dissonance and meticulous control became considerably more visceral onstage. Chaotic without feeling careless, this was a set that made it difficult to look away.

Kin Leonn x pureblue Ensemble

Credit: chrawme, courtesy of Esplanade – Theatres on the Bay

Kin Leonn x pureblue Ensemble took the collective's already intricate, ambient and contemporary compositions and gave them new depth. Joined by Bryan de Rozario on saxophone, Lucas Tee on drums and Mervin Wong on viola, the ensemble added breath, movement and physicality to music built on delicacy and restraint. Combined with the breathtaking visuals, every small detail seemed more textured and visceral, turning the performance into an incredibly immersive audiovisual experience. The result was a set that felt expansive, tactile, and completely absorbing.

Mediocre Haircut Crew

Credit: alvieisalive, courtesy of Esplanade – Theatres on the Bay

Mediocre Haircut Crew's return to Baybeats felt less like a comeback set and more like a block party with a few hundred friends. Backed by a full live band led by music director Kenzo Nagari, omarKENOBI, mickeyLEANO and daniKIDDO sounded bigger without losing the easy chemistry, impeccable live flow and stage charisma that have always made them such a fun act to watch. They debuted new material alongside favourites including 'Lose Your Love' and 'Fuck Da System', before ending with a full-crowd sing-along to 'WANNABES'. If there was any rust to shake off, you certainly couldn't hear it.

Srirajah Rockers

Credit: won997, courtesy of Esplanade – Theatres on the Bay

Srirajah Rockers brought a completely different kind of vibe to Baybeats — one driven by groove rather than sheer volume. The Thai veterans' blend of roots reggae, heavy dub, Thai soul, lovers rock, ska and funk unfolded with an easy confidence, leaving plenty of space for deep bass and laid-back rhythms to breathe. Warm, hypnotic and effortlessly danceable, the set showed why more than two decades together have made the group such an enduring presence in Thailand's reggae scene. Amid a weekend of wide-ranging sounds, Srirajah Rockers stood out by locking into an irresistible groove.

items.body: This ensemble will always carry a deeply personal connotation for me. In 2015, they released their first album, Rune , at a time when I was hospitalised for two weeks, waking at irregular hours. Despite the dire circumstances, listening to Earth Tongues at four in the morning, alone in the darkness, was a strange and deeply soothing experience. There was something about the ensemble’s careful, almost cautious little sounds—the tiny sonic points that gradually accumulated into a landscape that absorbed, captivated, and ultimately elevated you—that created a uniquely powerful listening experience. It is difficult to explain how important it became for me to return to this music again and again, and how much it taught me about the value of life, the value of art, and the value of improvised music. When everything collapses around you—and inside you—you begin to realise that whatever remains, however small or fragmented, can still be enough to create something meaningful. You learn to cherish the smallest isolated event - " at least I still have this ", to pay attention to what might otherwise go unnoticed, and to welcome the spontaneous connections with and between people who can, together, create beauty out of those tiny fragments of luck. And in many ways, that is what this music does. Little sounds, little fragments, little pieces surrounded by silence, which, when brought together, can still constitute something beautiful, something meaningful, something valuable. It gave me hope against all odds, and with it a profound insight: to cherish every moment. Life is not necessarily a long story with a clear plot. Perhaps it is instead a collection of small, random events—fragments that, taken together, become a life, and that are all worth living. The trio, so many years later are still Joe Moffett on trumpet, Dan Peck on tuba, and Carlo Costa on percussion. Like their previous albums, their sound is deeply organic, drawing on the textures and rhythms of the natural world: the drip of water, pebbles falling, animals growling, birds twittering. Each of the three long tracks has its own distinct character, while the music gradually evolves from pointillist blips into increasingly stretched-out tones in the final piece. Very slowly, almost imperceptibly, these scattered sonic fragments begin to coalesce. The subtlety of this shift is deliberate, shaped by carefully considered compositional ideas and structures. Silence is an essential part of their music—the white space between colours, an open realm of possibility waiting to be filled. What makes their work so compelling is the extraordinary value they give to each individual sound, with an intense attention to precision, texture, and timbral quality. When you enter their music attentively, it seems to slow down rational thought itself, allowing you to surrender to the sound and, for a while, simply be the music. items.body: Label: P&M Records, 2026 Personnel - Michael Blake: tenor and soprano saxophone; Gary Versace: piano; Ben Allison: bass; Michael Sarin: drums. Canadian-born, New York-based saxophonist and composer Michael Blake gathers a quartet of longtime collaborators for a slightly unsettling jazz session centered on Halloween, a holiday of imagination and transformation built around costumes, community, and the unexpected. Joining Blake here are pianist Gary Versace, bassist Ben Allison, and drummer Michael Sarin—all of whom have played and recorded with the saxophonist in various musical contexts. All nine compositions on the album are covers associated with Halloween, with the exception of the last track, Blake's " The Creep ", a shape-shifter showing many faces in minor mode with a bluesy feel. The opener, " Halloween ", slides in with mystery-induced suspense, leading to an atmospheric crescendo dreamily texturized by jagged piano chords in the high register. It keeps us engaged and alert as it moves forward in a fluid 5/4 time signature, strengthened by Blake's command of phrase and tone—he offers a haunting improvisation delivered with pure instinct and multiphonic impact. " Stalking Monster " and " Anatomy of a Murder " are Duke Ellington compositions, the former from Night Creature and the latter from Otto Preminger's film of the same name. " Stalking Monster " features tonally contrasting piano playing over hi-hat pulsation, creating eerie undertones before morphing into a 4/4 swing in the best that jazz tradition has to offer. An empowering feeling comes from the soloists: Blake is soulfully articulate while Versace introduces rich motivic ideas. This continuous fluidity, without straining to make a point, carries over to " Anatomy of a Murder ", a blues where bass and piano start in tandem, filling the lower register with gorgeous groove. The gears shift considerably on " The Great Pumpkin Waltz "—Vince Guaraldi's tune from the 1966 Halloween television special It's The Great Pumpkin, Charlie Brown —here delivered with harmonic sophistication and passionate lyricism. On soprano saxophone, Blake exudes clarity of technique and natural phrasing, switching to tenor on the following tune, " Transylvanian Lullaby ", the main haunting theme from Mel Brooks's 1974 comedy Young Frankenstein . Allison and Sarin build tension at the outset, and the piece becomes gently brushed after brief, well-devised staccato moves. The rhythm section compellingly swings in support of Blake's nimble solo. There's also a slow, rubato rendition of " Witchcraft ", Cy Coleman's tune popularized by Frank Sinatra and the Bill Evans Trio, where brooding melodicism comes to the fore. The chemistry between Blake and his rhythm team is undeniable throughout, even when the energy dips a bit after the first couple of tracks. Favorite Tracks: 01 - Halloween ► 02 - Stalking Monster ► 04 - Transylvanian Lullaby

items.body:
As touring productions grow more ambitious — and audiences increasingly expect the concert experience to begin long before the first song — venues are having to evolve alongside them. For Singapore EXPO, that evolution is taking shape through Apex @ EXPO, its enhanced large-format venue designed to accommodate audiences of up to 9,000.

The venue joins Arena @ EXPO, which caters to mid-sized productions, giving organisers greater flexibility across different capacities, configurations and technical requirements. With PLAVE and LE SSERAFIM among the acts bringing attention to the space, Apex @ EXPO also arrives as concert formats become increasingly technology-heavy and fan experiences extend beyond what happens on stage.

Bandwagon spoke with Ng Sim Lim, Vice President, Commercial at Constellar, which manages Singapore EXPO, about why the venue is expanding its live entertainment capabilities, what promoters are looking for today, and how fan expectations are reshaping the concert experience.

Why was this the right moment to enhance Apex @ EXPO, and what gaps in Singapore’s current live entertainment venue landscape were you hoping to address?

A few years ago, we identified a gap in Singapore's live entertainment landscape for venues catering to audiences in the 3,000 to 6,000 range. This led to the launch of Arena @ EXPO, which has established itself as a successful mid-sized concert venue for international live entertainment events, hosting major acts such as Mariah Carey, Westlife, RADWIMPS and NCT WISH. These events have contributed to the vibrancy of Singapore's entertainment scene while attracting regional fans who travel here for concerts.

Through Arena @ EXPO's success, we have gained valuable experience working closely with promoters and a better understanding of what it takes to deliver successful live entertainment events. At the same time, we saw growing demand for higher-capacity shows. The strong response to Arena @ EXPO gave us confidence that this was the right moment to enhance Apex @ EXPO and broaden the range of venue options available to organisers.

The enhancement of Apex @ EXPO comes at an opportune time, enabling us to cater to audiences of up to 9,000 while retaining the flexibility that organisers and promoters need. Together, Arena @ EXPO and Apex @ EXPO allow us to support a broader spectrum of live entertainment formats and audience sizes, from mid-sized shows of 3,000 to 6,000 attendees to larger-scale productions of up to 9,000 attendees.

This gives organisers greater flexibility to right-size their events while helping to address an important gap in Singapore's live entertainment venue landscape.

How important is that flexibility when promoters are deciding whether a production can work commercially in Singapore?

Flexibility is extremely important because every production comes with different audience profiles, operational and technical requirements, as well as commercial considerations.

Rather than committing to a fixed venue configuration, promoters increasingly look for spaces that can be adapted to suit the specific needs of a show. The ability to adjust capacities, seating layouts and stage configurations allows organisers to optimise both the audience experience and the commercial viability of an event.

At Apex @ EXPO, the venue can accommodate up to 7,572 attendees in a seated configuration, while replacing floor seats with a standing pen configuration can increase its total venue capacity to up to 9,000 attendees. This gives promoters greater flexibility to tailor the setup according to the nature of the event, expected attendance and overall programme objectives.

Beyond live entertainment, Apex @ EXPO is also well-suited for large-scale conferences, annual kick-offs and other business events. Organisers can leverage the venue's enhanced capabilities to create more impactful and immersive experiences for delegates.

As part of the Singapore EXPO ecosystem, Apex @ EXPO is also complemented by supporting facilities such as meeting rooms, registration areas and VIP holding spaces. This provides organisers with greater flexibility to utilise these spaces and design the overall event experience around their specific needs.

Ultimately, this versatility allows organisers and promoters to configure the venue in a way that best meets their objectives while delivering a high-quality experience for attendees.

With Apex @ EXPO and Arena @ EXPO now serving different audience sizes, how do you see the two venues complementing each other rather than competing for the same shows?

We see Apex @ EXPO and Arena @ EXPO as highly complementary offerings within Singapore EXPO's live entertainment portfolio.

Arena @ EXPO is well-suited for productions that require a more intimate audience experience, while Apex @ EXPO caters to larger-format events that can accommodate greater audience capacity, larger staging footprints and more extensive production setups.

More importantly, the distinction is not simply about audience numbers. Different productions have different technical requirements, creative ambitions and audience expectations. Having both venues allows us to offer organisers greater flexibility in selecting a space that best aligns with the needs of their event.

Together, Apex @ EXPO and Arena @ EXPO broaden the range of live entertainment experiences that can be hosted at Singapore EXPO.

What are international promoters and touring production teams asking for from venues today that they perhaps were not asking for five or ten years ago?

One of the biggest shifts is that promoters are evaluating venues far more holistically than before. Beyond capacity and technical specifications, factors such as production readiness, load-in efficiency, crowd management, transport connectivity and venue support have become increasingly important in the decision-making process.

Promoters today are looking not just for a venue, but for a venue partner that can help deliver a seamless experience from planning through to execution. They are also placing greater emphasis on flexibility, both operationally and commercially. Having the option to launch with a smaller event footprint and scale up where demand is strong allows promoters to better manage commercial risk while maximising opportunities for growth. This flexibility has become an increasingly important consideration when planning and delivering live entertainment events.

Audience expectations have also evolved significantly. Concertgoers today place greater value on convenience and the overall event experience, which means organisers are looking more closely at factors such as accessibility, food and beverage options, wayfinding and crowd flow.

At Singapore EXPO, concertgoers are also part of a wider event environment, with a variety of dining options and, from time to time, community, lifestyle and consumer experiences taking place across the venue. This creates a more vibrant atmosphere and allows attendees to make a day of their visit, rather than simply arriving for a performance and leaving immediately afterwards.

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by FriedRice Entertainment (@friedrice.live)

One of the first announced acts is virtual idol group PLAVE, whose performances can involve very different technological requirements from a conventional concert. Did preparing Apex @ EXPO involve thinking about increasingly digital, hybrid or technically complex live productions?

While Apex @ EXPO was not designed for any single act or production, we were very conscious of the fact that live entertainment is evolving rapidly, both in terms of audience expectations and production requirements.

Today, we are seeing a growing variety of formats, from traditional concerts and fan meetings to immersive experiences, virtual performances and productions that rely heavily on digital content and technology. Organisers increasingly require venues that can accommodate these different creative and technical demands.

The enhancement of Apex @ EXPO was therefore guided by a focus on versatility. Conceived as Singapore EXPO's next-generation multi-purpose venue, Apex @ EXPO was designed to support a wide range of production requirements, allowing organisers to adapt staging, audience configurations and technical setups according to the needs of each event.

In that sense, productions such as PLAVE demonstrate why adaptability is becoming increasingly important. As entertainment formats continue to evolve, venues need to be able to progress alongside them.

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by iMe SG 🇸🇬 (@ime.sg)

With LE SSERAFIM also among the early acts announced, K-pop is clearly an important part of the regional touring market. What have you learned from hosting K-pop productions about what fans and touring teams expect from venues today?

One of the key things we have observed is that K-pop audiences are incredibly engaged and invested in the overall event experience. The show and performing artistes remain the centrepiece, but fans are also paying close attention to everything surrounding the concert experience, from seamless queue management and merchandise collection to accessibility, food and beverage options, and how smoothly they can move through the venue.

We have also seen how venue capacity can influence the way K-pop acts engage with their audiences. While some of the artistes we host can easily fill a larger venue, a space such as Apex @ EXPO, with a capacity of up to 9,000, provides promoters with the option of staging multiple nights. This can create more opportunities for fans to attend, whether they are local fans hoping to catch more than one show or regional fans looking for dates that better fit their travel schedules.

As a result, organisers and touring teams are placing increasing emphasis on the entire fan journey rather than just what happens on stage. Fans today often arrive hours before a show begins and spend significant time at the venue before and after the performance, meeting fellow fans, taking photos, creating content and participating in fan-led activities. This makes the spaces and amenities around the venue just as important.

For touring teams, operational efficiency is equally important. They are looking for venues that can support complex production requirements while ensuring smooth crowd management, efficient load-ins and a positive experience for attendees.

In many ways, K-pop productions have raised the bar for live entertainment venues. They reinforce the idea that a successful event extends beyond the performance itself and is shaped by the overall experience fans have before, during and after the show.

The venue includes a sizeable pre-concert area for queues, security screening, F&B, merchandise and ticketing. How much attention is now being paid to the fan experience before and after the actual performance, rather than just what happens inside the concert hall?

A great deal of attention is now being paid to the experience before and after the performance itself. In many ways, the expectations of today's concertgoers have influenced how live event venues operate.

We observed this first-hand with Arena @ EXPO. One of the considerations behind the venue was ensuring that key front-of-house activities such as queueing, security screening, ticketing, merchandise collection and food and beverage offerings could take place comfortably within an indoor air-conditioned environment. In Singapore's climate, that can make a significant difference to the overall attendee experience.

We have also seen how these pre-concert areas can be used to create richer event experiences beyond the performance itself. For instance, at Mediacorp's CLOUD 9 Music Festival, which took place at Arena @ EXPO this May, organisers transformed the venue into a festival-like environment with brand and sponsor activations, giving attendees opportunities to engage with the event well before the show started. This allowed fans to immerse themselves in the experience from the moment they arrived, rather than simply coming for the performance.

The same thinking has influenced Apex @ EXPO. Beyond the performance space itself, organisers have access to generous areas that can support queue management, merchandise operations, security screening and other event-day activities. These spaces allow organisers to better manage audience flow while providing attendees with a more comfortable and seamless experience.

We are also looking at how the wider Singapore EXPO destination can add to the fan experience. For selected concerts, our on-site Korean-style self-photo booth studio offers exclusive customised concert-themed photo frames, giving fans another way to capture and share memories from the event.

Ultimately, venues today are expected to support much more than the performance itself. Increasingly, organisers are looking at how every part of the venue contributes to the success of the event, from the moment attendees arrive to the moment they leave.

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by Singapore EXPO (@singaporeexpo)

When a 9,000-capacity audience leaves a show at roughly the same time, transport and crowd movement become part of the concert experience too. How has Singapore EXPO planned for arrivals, departures and crowd flow at larger entertainment events?

Crowd management and transport planning are critical considerations for any large-scale event, whether it is a conference, exhibition or live entertainment concert.

One of Singapore EXPO's key advantages is that it was originally designed to accommodate large volumes of visitors across a wide range of event formats. The venue benefits from direct MRT connectivity, extensive parking facilities, dedicated drop-off points and multiple access routes, all of which help to support smoother crowd movement before and after an event.

Managing large crowds is also not new to us. Over the years, Singapore EXPO has successfully hosted some of Singapore's largest exhibitions, consumer events and gatherings, with attendance figures exceeding 50,000 visitors. In this light, crowd flow, queue management and visitor movement have long been part of our operational DNA.

We also have the benefit of significant space across the venue precinct, which helps organisers manage queueing, security screening and audience dispersal more effectively. Every event is planned according to its specific requirements, but the overall objective remains the same: to ensure attendees can move safely, comfortably and efficiently throughout their event experience.

Ultimately, a successful live event is not just about what happens on stage. It is also about ensuring that the journey to and from the venue is as seamless as possible for audiences.

Finally, beyond K-pop and major international pop concerts, are there particular genres, formats or types of productions that you believe Apex @ EXPO will allow Singapore to host more frequently?

One of Apex @ EXPO's strengths is its versatility. While live entertainment is an important growth area for us, the venue was originally designed as a large-format plenary space capable of supporting keynote sessions, conferences and business events at scale.

As a result, Apex @ EXPO is well-positioned to support a broad spectrum of productions beyond concerts. This includes theatrical performances, live shows, large-scale presentations, fan conventions, cultural showcases, immersive experiences and other formats that require substantial audience capacity and production capabilities.

Rather than being purpose-built for a single genre or event type, Apex @ EXPO was designed to be adaptable. That gives organisers the flexibility to reimagine the space according to their creative and production requirements.

We believe this versatility will create opportunities for Singapore to host a wider range of experiences, particularly productions that may not fit neatly into traditional venue categories.

items.body:
After the OĽUN album I reviewed enthusiastically a while back, here’s the next project, again motivated and led by violinist/fiddler/composer Ján Kružliak Jr., continuing the rapprochement, indeed embrace, between Slovakia’s traditional music and its classical music. This time it reconnects the works of classical composers who were inspired by and drew on village musics with those traditional sources and styles.
Three ensembles are involved: the Spectrum Quartett led by Kru�liak with two violins, viola and cello; Nogaband, the traditional-style quartet of fiddles, contra (chording viola) and bass that’s led by fiddler and singer Michal Noga; and the female vocal group Ulijanky, plus guest singer Simona Hulejov�.
The majority of the tracks are interpretations of works by Slovak composer Eugen Suchon (1908-1993), with others from fellow-Slovaks Ilja Zeljenka (1932-2007) and Alexander Moyzes (1906-1984), and Hungarian B�la Bart�k (1881-1945) who did a lot of his very detailed collecting of folk music in Slovakia.
In each case the sources - musicians and locations in villages across Slovakia - are credited in the notes, and these arrangements and performances reconnect with the energy and traditional vocal sound of those sources.
In no way is this an orchestra-smoothed thing; this is gutsy, brilliantly played and sung music with all the spirit, skill and technique of traditional music, from players and singers who deeply understand and inhabit it. It’s a glorious piece of work, music to luxuriate in. There’s too much richness to begin to detail, but here’s a dip into a few moments to give the flavor. The tracks all have very long titles detailing their sources, so for brevity’s sake I’ll just give track numbers.

items.body: Karine Polwart has proved herself to be an exceptional talent as a singer and songwriter for many years, all the way back to her time with Malinky (the song �Thaney� was a revelation). As a solo artist she�s grown and continually expanded her horizons, coming now to Windblown , a project that began life seven years ago, when Polwart, along with sound designer and composer Pippa Murphy, was artist in residence at Royal Botanic Garden Edinburgh. The album, with its stage show and book, tells the story of the garden�s oldest specimen, a Sabal palm tree ( Sabal bermudana ), which was gently felled in 2021, and contained a surprise nobody had expected. The tree is the starting point. From there, imagination runs free. Windblown by Karine Polwart & Pippa Murphy featuring Dave Milligan It�s an album of voice and piano (the outstanding, sympathetic Dave Milligan), and, for all its global outlook on connections, one that�s very rooted in Scotland. You can hear it on the opening track, �Hear The Rigging/Last In Line,� where the melody becomes a slow, aching lament that would sound completely natural on the pipes. The stripped-down sound gives the songs both crafted stateliness and real intimacy. Each one is an exhalation, a memory, a celebration and exploration, with recurring phrases in the words and music acting as touchstones � or even hooks; they certainly stick in the mind. Windblown by Karine Polwart & Pippa Murphy featuring Dave Milligan In many ways, this is a modest album, with piano, voice and light, judicious soundscaping. It won�t overpower with noise. Yet at the same time, it�s epic, a look at history, at the flow and grandeur of nature, and the things we all carry within us. The music, and especially Polwart�s warm, compassionate voice, envelop the listener, and makes them a participant, not an observer, but a part of the journey and the history. Windblown by Karine Polwart & Pippa Murphy featuring Dave Milligan The irony arrives at the end, when the venerable old tree is down, and seeds are examined. What people for two hundred years had believed to be a Sabal bermudana turns out to be something different, a Sabal mexicana � and one of the small plants fill grow where it�s forerunner once stood. Windblown by Karine Polwart & Pippa Murphy featuring Dave Milligan Like music, plants keep to a different time � and this album/book/show give the tree the requiem it deserves, as well as hope for the future. They speak of the earth, the sun, the moon, stars and planets, of lost brothers, quarrelling sisters, loss and grief, of the power of imagination, and of the answers to the simplest and most difficult riddles.� The lyrics of all the songs, in Norwegian, are included in the sleeve notes and while a hasty online translation can aid with some understanding, the full meanings tend to remain cryptic, but there is a sense that words and music complement each other. For example, Slovenian-native R�n�lius Bikar�s searing violin opens the set with �R�fuge.� He and his self-named ensemble channel pan-European Roma history.
Meanwhile, �Poor Boy� is a Django Reinhardt-inspired swing tune by Charlotte Pelgen & Bipolar Bows. Pelgen sings in English, and with her ukulele strumming sounding very much like a tenor banjo, the tune is enlivened by Lotte Remmen�s St�phane Grappelli-like fiddle lines.
The distinctive sound of the oud announces yet another musical tradition. Blending Mediterranean with Arabic sounds, the Lebanese-Belgian singer Amber Haddad and her trio, oudist Adil Benhsain and double bassist Martijn Vanbuel, spin a beguiling musical web. According to the liner notes (translated from the Dutch), �Tawazden� is about �seeking balance and finding peace within a complex environment.� Further, �the various spaces of the abbey and their murals are the direct source of inspiration.�
The accordion is especially prominent. So too is the Western classical tradition. Sounding almost Baroque, �Sacristia Invisibilis,� is another standout for me. Here, mandolinist Andries Boone is joined by Anouk Sanczuk on octave violin (sometimes called the baritone violin, tuned an octave lower than standard) and on harpsichord Sandra Van der Gucht. They create an indescribable sound you have to hear.
Throughout, the Abbey�s stone presence looms. Aur�lie Charneux�s solo clarinet piece �L'Ape Millenaria� is about a thousand-year-old bee that haunts the abbey. �Thila,� by Enara Navaira, evokes ancient Celts with a jazzy double bass and drum kit behind throat singing and Citera (a kind of Hungarian zither).
Airboxes is a duo who mix chromatic and diatonic accordions. Their offering �Abdij 1� sounds improvised. Again from the liner notes, �they share their impressions of the timelessness of monastic life.�

has a coherence, perhaps informed by the artists� shared inspiration. The record is often surprising and always soothing. Three years in the making, the ensembles were lovingly recorded and mixed by Bert Huysentruyt and mastered by Pieter De Wagter from Equus Mastering. items.body: "There is no such thing as a stranger�s children." - old Ukrainian saying I�ve long been affected, indeed somewhat obsessed, by what�s happening in Ukraine, partly because of one of my favorite bands, DakhaBrakha. I went to Kyiv to see them at the time of the Maidan protests, just after the shooting by snipers of over a hundred protesters. I intentionally didn�t read this album�s booklet notes before listening, so that I could react to it without sympathetic pre-judgement, just as music. It�s strong musically and vocally by any standards, Ukrainian or otherwise. When I did then turn to the notes that translate and explain the songs, I had that rare experience, for me, of becoming moist-eyed. The songs are a mix of traditional and original. They are focused on the abduction by Russia of about 20,000 Ukrainian children who have been taken from their parents in Russian-occupied eastern Ukraine and sent to Russia, in an attempt to turn them into haters of their native land and people. It�s a heinous war crime. Marichka is a Ukrainian-Canadian singer who moves between Canada and her homeland. For this album she�s gathered two groups of musicians, one in each country. Both ensembles contribute vocals and instrumentation, mostly bowed strings, plus some bandura and piano. The group in Ukraine includes Lisa from the destroyed and invaded city of Mariupol, playing a solo on double ocarina; at 16 she was one of the stolen children but managed to return to Ukraine. Daughters of Donbas � co-led by Marichka and singer/bandurist Alina Kuzma, who shares the lead vocal role � is an all-female ensemble in Canada that tours performing these songs. �Foreign Land� is a reworking of a traditional song about the young girls who were sent away to work in foreign households - Marichka�s grandmother was one of these - that can also be taken to refer to the plight of today�s stolen children. The translation goes: A mother packed up her daughter To leave for a strange land To a strange land with strange people Oh, who will pity you, my daughter? Those who will beat me will pity me I'll never again live with you, my mother When, my daughter, should I expect you to come home? When the grass in the garden grows, my mother The grass grew and grew and began to dry The mother was waiting for her daughter to return, and began to cry Did you hear, my mother, how I came to you? How I flew as a bird above your window? How I cooed like a dove? If, my daughter, I could hear you I would open all the doors and windows To let you fly in Songs of Stolen Children by Daughters of Donbas, Alina Kuzma, Zo� Santo As befits the song, Marichka�s vocal here is gentle. But in the second track, �Rusalka,� with Alina Kuzma taking the lead vocals, things turn harsh and fierce. A rusalka is a mythical creature, a nature spirit of fields, forest and rivers, that features in traditional ritual songs. The melody of this one is by Zo� Santo and Kuzma, with lyrics drawing on tradition and the composition of Santo and 19thC Ukrainian poet and folklorist Taras Shevchenko. An ominous double-bass drone, chunking strings, a slithering vocal that moves into sections of white-voice fast recitative and expands into a soaring wild cry. The lyrics are very dark, perhaps evoking the hell of the front line: Home a hell of old growth stumps Marsh a mud of memories Don�t get bogged down in these parts Your kind won�t last a day in here While witches still fly, while roosters have yet to crow, Come here, something arises, �neath the oak something walks. A rusalka sat on a white birch, rusalky asked girls for shirts. Long fingers and nails so sharp Tongue forked round serrated teeth Moss grows down beneath her parts Weeds braided from ear to ear While witches still fly, while roosters have yet to crow, Come here, something arises, �neath the oak something walks. �Girls, my friends, give me your shirts. Though I�m thin, give me a thin one.� Here live us the backless ones Many voices of dead sons You are right to quake in fear Send your sinful children here �Who Am I� is a plea of separation and disorientation, the pain and confusion of an abducted child, contrasting �the human in me� and �the creature in me,� like an internalized riddle-song, with the refrain, in English: Who am I for you? Who am I for me? Do you know me? Really know me? �Enchantress,� passionately sung by Kuzma to her own bandura accompaniment, a girl�s lament of the loss of her brave love taken from her by the enchantress, who is an allegory of war, is based on a traditional song and uses that style of melody and lyrics, �Riddle,� sung by Marichka, reworks a traditional riddle song to be the riddles told by the grandfather of a child, 12-year-old Kira from Mariupol, who experienced the death of her father and her abduction to Russia. Her grandfather tracked her down, and brought her back, traumatized, and asked her riddles - as the notes say �to jog her memory, and remind her who she was, where her home was, and of her family�s love for her.� Songs of Stolen Children by Daughters of Donbas, Marichka �4.5.0� is a military expression for �all�s well� or �all is quiet.� The song is a message, as from a mother, to a stolen child. Marichka�s voice is cherishing: Remember this: I am with you, I am here Don't give up, I'm with you. Don't give up, I'm with you Your hope is my weapon Don't be sad, I'm with you 4.5.0. will be again �breaking into a tearing howl: And when the world's axis breaks When the sky folds like a parchment Out of nowhere her words will come� �and back to fragile reassurance �It's all right, I'm here, I'm here� "Lullaby," based on a traditional lullaby, sung by Alina Kuzma to accompaniment by her bandura and Zo� Santo's viola, starts in gentle lullaby style, but moves to a lament; it's for the stolen children and those who, as the notes put it, 'have been stolen for ever.' Songs of Stolen Children by Daughters of Donbas, Marichka �Remember, I Believe in You� is a powerful piece of harmonizing vocals and slithering strings. Here�s the story it�s based on: Yevhen lived in Mariupol with his three young children. During the siege they lived in a basement bomb shelter for months. One day, Russian soldiers entered their bomb shelter. Yevhen was taken to a filtration camp and separated from his children who were all taken to a hospital and then to Russian summer �camp�. In the filtration camp Yevhen was brutally tortured and forced to sleep standing on one leg. He tried to fall asleep, whispering prayers for his children: �Everything will be fine, I believe in you.� After his release he walked 30 kilometers to the place where his children had been taken but it was too late. They had already been sent to Moscow. Yevhen learned of this after receiving a text from one of his children who had found an unattended device. He traveled thousands of kilometers, crossed the borders of three countries, endured checks, interrogations and danger to reach Moscow and take his children home. All those days he tirelessly repeated to himself, �I believe in myself, I believe in my kids. Everything will be good.� �Another Heaven,� sung by Marichka with the ensemble in Ukraine, is inspired by another heart-rending story: Ilya was 9 years old when his mother was killed by a rocket strike right in front of him. He was taken to a hospital in occupied Donetsk, where 15 pieces of shrapnel were removed from his body without anesthesia. After he appeared in a report on Russian television, Ilya�s grandmother learned his location. She managed to bring her grandson to Kyiv, where he lives now, experiencing missile attacks every night. At age 11, he says that it is up to everyone to fight enemies, to protect other cities, and to build another heaven, where your home will not be destroyed. In 2014, during the Kyiv Maidan protests, Marichka wrote and performed �Red Boots Tango,� using a melody she�d put to a poem by Taras Shevchenko. For this album she sings it again in Ukraine, with the ensemble there adding swirling, classic tango-style strings. Songs of Stolen Children by Daughters of Donbas, BanduraGirl The final track on the album is a solo, recorded in Kyiv, by Anastasiya Voytyuk, accompanying herself on the older, simpler form of bandura that was used by kobzars to accompany epic poetry, and also on the nowadays more well-known big, heavy form developed from it in Soviet times that was made mainly in the piano factory at Chernihiv. Her song, �Soon I Will Be Back,� is based on a poem by novelist, journalist and war crime researcher Victoria Amelia, who was killed in 2023, in the city of Kramatorsk in Donbas, by a Russian rocket. items.body: Palagoma is not only the first release from Nairobi-based label Cool Waters, it also marks the first time German-born, Kenya-based percussionist Sven Kacirek has collaborated with Ogoya Nengo and Olith Ratengo at the same time. Odd Okoddo, the duo of Kacirek and Ratengo, has been performing since 2018, but with the inclusion of the 83 year old Nengo, a singer from the eastern part of the country, there�s an added traditional depth to the music. A 2025 performance shows Nengo�s lifetime of experience singing Kenya�s dodo tradition around 2 and half minutes in (see below). Furthermore, her inclusion on this album allows her and Ratengo to toss the vocals back and forth as they reference their shared roots (Ratengo and Nengo live minutes from each other). Musically, however, the tracks are driven by Kacirek�s Buchla synth, hand percussion, and occasional kit drumming, which serve to buoy the voices without blotting out the music�s origins. Palagoma by Odd Okoddo & Ogoya Nengo �Bara,� for example, begins with the dime-store thwack of a repeated pattern, a stiff juxtaposition to the voices; yet, as the song rolls along, a 4/4 clink appears, then a burbling bass, and finally, what sounds like a xylophone. Layers of synthesized polyrhythms keep presenting themselves with a subtlety almost unnoticeable, until, by the track�s end, it feels organic, as if it�s all been underneath the two voices all along. Palagoma by Odd Okoddo & Ogoya Nengo �Sarah,� perhaps the album�s most intense track, features a lead vocal from Ratengo and tentative, percussive spittles from Kacirek. And while the technology never tries to overtake the vocals, it does sneak up and punctuate the track�s urgency, as edgy distortion sneaks in here and there just as Ratengo�s voice reaches its peak. The term �folktronica� has been bandied about as a way to house the type of music on offer here. In fact, exploratory collaborations such as Chouk Bwa & The �ngstr�mers as well as much of Kampala, Uganda�s Nyege Nyege label house sounds that might be �folktronic� in some way. What�s more interesting and important about this music, though, is how truly global so much of it is while maintaining a deep connection to Africa and its diasporic communities. The music on Palagoma , as well as much of what�s linked above (and available in countless other recent recordings) demonstrates a real willingness for cultures to respond to each other without trampling traditions altogether. Instead, roots become avant-garde and innovations become seemingly thousands of years old. Certainly the inclusion of an 83 year old traditional Kenyan singer only recently making her global debut as she tours with a duo whose instrumental voice is a white male saturated in electronic Kenyan rhythms demonstrates this blurring. The music this trio makes is certainly of the 21st century, but it�s often hazy, sparse, and open, keeping it from a quick sell-by date or confining it to a specific genre. Instead, it�s a beautiful example music as grace.

items.body:
According to its founder, Eugene Rodriguez, who also sings and plays on the record, Los Cenzontles is a �musical group and non-profit organization, which I founded over thirty years ago.�  As he continues in the album�s liner notes, the group �has a long history of producing projects exploring Mexico�s deep roots and our connections with various traditions that, so far, have included Irish, Louisiana Creole, Cuban, American cowboy, classical, pop, rock, and blues�, the latest of which is
Adios Ke Aloha: Waves of the Same Sea
. Los Cenzontles translates to the mockingbird, or, from its Aztec root word, the bird of four hundred voices. This is a fitting name for the range of musical diversity represented here.
With songs sung in Spanish, Hawaiian, and English, the concept traces back to the legacy of Mexican cowboys who travelled from California to the Hawaiian Islands to wrangle the long-horned cattle introduced there in the nineteenth century. They also brought the guitar. The 16 tracks feature old Hawaiian songs with new Spanish lyrics, old Mexican songs with new Hawaiian lyrics, new compositions, and traditional Americana. Yet it is an entirely cohesive musical package held together by dense arrangements of ukuleles, guitars, Mexican harp, and accordion.
Sonny Lim & David Hidalgo
Besides their distinctive voices, the headline artists Taj Mahal and David Hidalgo provide the gravitas and musicianship that their long and distinguished careers have earned. According to the liner notes, they were the catalysts behind the project and facilitated the choice of songs, arrangements, and played a range of instruments. On vocals they are joined by Hawaiian natives Gary Haleamau, Sheldeen Haleamau, Sonny Lim, and long-time Cenzontles member Fabiola Trujillo.
Deportee
To give a taste of the sessions, included before the traditional �Fishin� Blues� is Taj Mahal teaching the musicians how to play it. Sung by David Hildalgo,  the lovely �A Matter of Time� comes from the 1984 album
Will the Wolf Survive
by his most famous project, Los Lobos. Another standout for me, �Navegar� features a slack string guitar solo reminiscent of Duane Eddie and one of many tasty lap steel turns by Sonny Lim. Their interpretation of Woody Guthrie's �Deportee� moves into social commentary, highlighting the cruel realities of being a migrant worker in America.
Vaquero Paniolo
Recorded over five days, mostly live in one room at the Los Cenzontles headquarters in San Pablo, California, including the talents of some of their academy�s students, the recording has real spontaneity to it. Arrangements are stretched by improvisations, sometimes by several different instruments on a single tune. The project also represents a great spirit of cooperation and diversity of language, culture, age, and gender. It includes the inputs of musical legends, seasoned pros, and amateurs. The wonderfully rich and often stereotyped musical cultures of both Mexico and Hawaii are represented here with the authenticity of lived experience.
Adios Ke Aloha: Waves of the Same Sea
is a worthy addition to Los Cenzontles� important work. Quoting Rodriguez again, �Culture is a fabric within which we are all woven.�

items.body: For an overview of the what, the why, and the where of this music, do read my review of Volume 1 of this series. Essentially, this collection is more of what made Volume 1 so infectious. Yet, what makes this music so fascinating in general, that is, beyond its unswerving ability to fill dance floors, is the fact that these two islands, part of the Paises Africanos de Lingua Oficial Portuguesa (PALOP) regions of the world, are the second smallest African country; Seychelles is smaller. There are only 12 villages on Sao Tom�, lots of rain forest and, not surprisingly, lots of rain. I mention this because one could be fooled into thinking, with music like what�s on offer here, there must have been a music scene larger than there actually was. Not that little was happening, but that less got recorded or released than it might have had there been a city such as Lagos or Nairobi with the studios, labels, and pressing plants to better document it all. The music here, like Volume 1- recorded during Africa�s so-called golden age- is known as Puxa, a complex stew of ingredients from other former African Portuguese colonies mixed with rhythms that, with the help of dancers, can summon spirits or exorcise demons. At least according to some. It�s worth knowing that a 100 years or so ago, the Portuguese banned Puxa dance; it�s also worth knowing they appear to have failed miserably at this silly endeavor. Tucked away in modern Puxa is merengue, Kompas, Soukouss, Benga, and much else. One suspects much of this is coincidental, while other grooves were definitely imported considering both Portuguese rule and the islands� location over the Atlantic from the Caribbean. But don�t be fooled into thinking these two islands don�t have their own thing, as the sounds on this collection show. L�VE L�VE Vol. 2: Sao Tom� & Principe Sounds 70s-80s - Pedro Lima Pedro Lima, who has featured in his own Bongo Joe collection, leads a fiery band, complete with choked guitar vamps tussling with a kit drummer as a lead guitar comments from the sidelines on �Sossegado.� Elsewhere, Sangazuza demonstrates what happens when the bass and keys drop out, leaving the drummers and guitars to ride out a groove and drive dancers mad in the process. Check �Sono s� ku� de t�ma� or �Mairo bi cedo� for their ability to place a firm finger on the pulse. Over 15 tracks, the collection shows off multiple guitars weaving and circling one another, with lead and harmony vocals constantly in response, becoming part of the songs� melodic framework. At any given moment, vocals give way as the music unspools and floats on grooves that must have gone on for hours live. Africa Negra�s �Apoi�mos a luta dos nossos irm�os� is one example. L�VE L�VE Vol. 2: Sao Tom� & Principe Sounds 70s-80s by Various Artists In general, what�s on offer here, like Volume 1, was recorded at Radio Sao Tom� e Principe (RSTP), often taped in the courtyard outside at night, and released on cassette or occasionally, vinyl. It captures the joy of post-1975 independence and only fizzled out as styles changed and musicians struggled to make ends meet. Yet, take a quick listen to recent RSTP programming, which features musicians such as Babilonia or Calema, and you�ll still hear Puxa rhythms, showing just how potent the music form this two-island nation is on a global level. And Bongo Joe, who have also released two volumes featuring the above mentioned Africa Negra, have given this music the treatment it deserves, with extensive notes on the country�s history, vintage photographs, and band discographies. items.body: Known for playing with County Joe McDonald, and for her experimental sound band The United States of America, Dorothy Moskowitz came back in 2023 with United States of Alchemy and their well-received release, Under an Endless Sky . In collaboration with avant-garde composer and filmmaker Francesco Paolo Paladino, and poet and music writer Luca Chino Ferrari, Songs of Compassion is eleven songs containing subversive and at times beautiful music, and richly evocative lyrics. Francesco Paolo Paladino and Luca Chino Ferrari | Photo by Maria Assunta Karini Songs of Compassion has two challenges for the listener. The first is the music, called variously avant-garde, ambient, modal, non-linear, and a few more. It is played mostly on pianos mixed in and out of the foreground, sometimes doubled, and sometimes out of phase, joined by strings, woodwinds, synth washes, and steely sounds. Initially disorienting, the music serves to remind us how locked our minds are to Western notions of harmonic movement. It speaks of alternative musical narratives much older and much further away. They are songs that subvert the song: more like Steve Reich than Steve Stills; more like Phillip Glass than Phil Collins. UNITED STATES OF ALCHEMY - Pale Wanderer At the same time, there are the poetic yet strikingly contemporary lyrics. �Pale Wanderer� talks about the fact that authoritarianism needs willing accomplices, describing what happens �When you make a deal with darkness.� UNITED STATES OF ALCHEMY (Dorothy Moskowitz, Francesco Paolo Paladino e Luka Chino Ferrari) by Silentes �Charlottesville� (written with the late Joe Byrd) evokes the time not long ago when torch-wielding nazis, proud of the metaphoric Ns on their tunics, chanted the antisemitic tropes paraphrased in Moskowitz�s words, �We�ll be one people, pure of race/No greedy throng could take our place� . Besides the overtly political lyrics, in the tradition of 1960s protest songs, there are also thoughtful meditations on mortality and our place in the universe. The message is high-minded yet sincere and direct. World weary and wise, Moskowitz�s voice inhabits the evocative philosophical lyrics with the authority of a skilled method actor. The melodies unfold like streams of consciousness, rising and falling, not following expected diatonic chord progressions, but honouring, instead, the value of each word. Moskowitz�s piano acts as another voice and sometimes a kind of Greek chorus commenting on the proceedings. The surrounding music frames, creates pulses and dissonances, and shimmers. The return of Dorothy Moskowitz with her renamed project has arrived in a moment quite similar to the times that spawned its predecessor. Political division, unrest, and uncertainty always generate artistic reaction, and United States of Alchemy roared back to life with their epic 24-minute opening track �Under an Endless Sky� in 2023, serving perhaps as an �In-A-Gadda-Da-Vida� for our times. Songs of Compassion continues to challenge how we think about our world. It�s music that defies the song form, while doing exactly what music is supposed to do�enrich the human condition. items.body: Those of us who have been digging into Analog Africa�s increasingly formidable releases over the last two decades are well aware of the massive amount of raw, vodun-based Sato and Sakpata-derived funk the label has issued by Benin�s most prolific 1970s-era band, the Orchestre Poly-Ritmo. AA has dropped no fewer than 3 compilations of their heaviest material, as well as a reissue of the band�s first LP, in an effort to give them the international status they deserve. That being said, what might be different about this collection of their music? And who is Antoine Dougb�? Antoine Dougb� et L'Orchestre Poly-Rythmo De Cotonou 1977 - 1982 (Analog Africa No.44) by Analog Africa As it turns out, Dougb� was a song-conjurer whose mode of musical transfer was slapping his legs in a rhythm known as Cavacha, a groove created by drummer Belobi Meridjo, who was inspired by a train cadence that he worked into a pattern that ultimately spread like a 21st century California wildfire throughout Congolese pop music in the mid-1970s. Dougb�, known as the �Devil�s Prime Minister,� was also a practitioner of vodun who inspired fear in any musician he felt was unsuited to play his music, which is how he landed on working exclusively Poly-Ritmo, as he felt they could nail what he wanted in ways other bands couldn�t. His recording career was brief - 3 albums and a few singles - but as this collection shows, it was potent. Antoine Dougb� et L'Orchestre Poly-Rythmo De Cotonou 1977 - 1982 (Analog Africa No.44) by Analog Africa Because of the era from which this music dates, it�s not surprising that the recording and instrument tones have changed - the guitars have a plastic sheen and synthesizers appear- even if the music remains rooted in the 1970s. Perhaps the influence of the Cuban son is more apparent here than on other Poly-Ritmo collections, especially in the collection�s initial offerings. And yes, Congolese rumba, then shaking all of sub-Saharan Africa to its knees, is present too. �Ma Won Min Towe Leo� is one example. Opening with a bed of synthesizers, the shimmering guitars, tinny, seemingly squeezed dry by the 80s themselves, lock in over relentless high-hat-focused grooves. The guitars finally start firing in different directions midway through, before that synth weaves back in, forming a bed underneath it all. Antoine Dougb� et L'Orchestre Poly-Rythmo De Cotonou 1977 - 1982 (Analog Africa No.44) by Analog Africa �We Tayi Sin Assi Tche� is much more overtly Cuban. With its insistent cowbell, classic, nasal vocal call and response, and tight, repeated guitar figures, its debt to mid-twentieth century Afro-Cuban sons is transparent. Another track, �Djomido Ma Dougbe Tche� rides a groove reminiscent of 70�s-era Franco classic �Liberte.� The pulse is relentless, and the guitar solo repeats a tight repetition of a few notes, driving listeners to ecstasy all the while. However, none of this music is a mere copy of its influences; rather, like so much potent pop coming from the continent at the time, it is a swirl of major influences rendered by local rhythms and vocal phrasing to give it specific identity, in this case, to Benin. Dougb�s musical role on this collection is a bit murky. One of his three albums has a photo of him, fully mic�d behind a collection of hand drums, so perhaps he served as a percussionist/vocalist; this release never explains. He wasn�t a songwriter in the traditional sense. It seems he was more of an instigator and arranger, but his thumbprint was apparently heavy enough to warrant his name on the records he was involved with. Whatever the case, in his brief run as a recording artist, he and Poly-Ritmo produced a handful of driving, Cavacha-inspired grooves that can still wear holes in club floors. items.body: Tako Toki are like desert island musicians who, castaway without their instruments, were forced to construct their own. Lucky for us, they are as skilled in making instruments as they are in creating original songs with which to show off their handicrafts. Un Dimanche � Monaco is the band�s follow-up to their well-received debut, Hirsute Farfelus , with a similar mash of musical styles. Before discussing the music, we need to talk about their instrument closet. They really have built everything they play out of bric-a-brac, odds and ends, and rubbish. I�m not sure from listening which is which, but they call their instruments, in an incomplete list, tassofons, tilofons, and tubofones, clarinuts, didjerimou, and klarbass, and my favorite, kitchenofon. (I will refer to what I hear by the names of store-bought instruments that they sound like.) The most surprising thing for me was how accurate the instruments were to pitch and how good they sounded under the harsh scrutiny of modern recording microphones that have documented a rich, high-quality sound. UN DIMANCHE A MONACO - LP by Tako Toki They have also very effectively matched their choice of instruments with the style of music that inspires their compositions. Right off the top, �Yinitza� features a laughing clarinet singing a klezmer tune accompanied by bassoon for the bass, frantic two-time percussion, and the exuberant human yelps found on many klezmer recordings. As on this track, many tunes feature improvisations that show an impressive degree of musicianship. On the cumbia-inspired �Le Cuenta,� the characteristic flute carries the tune, augmented by a Spanish singing chorus, and remarkably rich-sounding Latin percussion. The title track surrounds us with afrobeat woodblocks, shakers, and rattles scattered around the mix. The melody is played on a marimba ornamented with bells and cymbals. Again, the lead player improvises over the tune and often against the beat with jazzy chops. The flute returns on the samba-inspired �Ambiguidade,� and on �Aksum� it traces a trance-like Middle Eastern tune reminiscent of a 60s TV spy-show theme. UN DIMANCHE A MONACO - LP by Tako Toki Full of fun and one of a kind, Un Dimanche � Monaco celebrates our universal love of rhythmic, melodic, and harmonic sounds and the varied, wonderful ways cultures have organized that love in what we call music. At the same time, playing on literal pieces of junk, Tako Tiko reminds us, as we contemplate many mall music shops filled with gleaming wood and brass instruments and countless unused guitars lying in closets, that musicians will always find a way to make music. Over a few glasses of marc, to continue to speculate, they conjured up the idea for Les Primitifs du futur.  Since then, they have recorded an impossible-to-categorize series of albums, with cover illustrations by Crumb, of which Les Crimes du Mussette is the fifth.
Weird and wonderful, it sounds like they rooted through an attic full of 78 RPM records, scribbled down some arrangements, and then played them on a collection of instruments they found in another attic, including accordion, sax, xylophone, clarinet, banjo, ukulele, theremin, Hawaiian guitar, bagpipe chanter (I�m guessing here), and musical saw.
Ne tirez pas sur le pianiste (excerpt)
The 27 short tracks are mostly voiced by Cravic, who talk-sings in the manner of an everyman Maurice Chevalier. He is often accompanied by the accordion, a customary instrument in the bal-musette style that remains a strong element of the eclectic range of styles they have managed to synthesize. They also include ragtime, jug, French chanson, and, to my ears, skiffle,  just to get the list started.
Ukulele Lady (excerpt)
The liner notes point out that �Les Crimes du Musette is also a gold mine for scholars, a veritable treasure trove.� Exploring the treasures is beyond my scope here, as each tune has a long history. A highlight for me is the humorous �Ukulele Lady� from 1925, which first delighted me on Arlo Guthrie�s 1971 album

. The song has also been covered by Bing Crosby, Peter Sellers, and Bette Midler.

A more serious item is �N�oublie pas Gr�co� (Don�t Forget Gr�co�)  is a tribute to the legendary chanteuse and heroine of the French Resistance, Juliette Gr�co, who died in 2020. This record is a curiosity, but it is performed by serious musicians with total commitment. In this, I was reminded of the similarly indefinable Dan Hicks & the Hot Licks. Tiny Sun creates tiny songs that give off light and heat well out of proportion to their size. Composed, performed, and produced by Martina Sorbara, Jonathan Goldsmith, and Don Rooke, the record is vaguely Americana, with plucked guitars and ukuleles, chiming keyboards, and the lonesome slide of the guitar.
Vanishment
contains eighteen sparkling miniatures - that take a scant 34 minutes to negotiate - notable for their economy of arrangement and the subtle directness of the lyrics. The tracks glow with Martina�s clear, high, and sometimes fragile voice.
The songs are about loss: lost love, lost confidence, but sometimes about resignation to the enigmatic quirks of the world. The tone of wry fatalism mirrors the fact that this project is the work of many years of collaboration and email exchanges while the trio pursued their musical day jobs. Jonathan Goldsmith is an award-winning composer for television and film, Don Rooke fronts the Toronto roots band The Henrys, and Martina Sorbara is known for folk, electropop, and her band Dragonette.
Kerosene Madrigal
The range of backgrounds leads to many styles, and the record betrays interesting influences. The opening track, �Kerosene Madrigal,� is a sort of miner�s blues reminiscent of Michelle Shocked. The soul-country of �Imagined Love� reminded me of fellow Torontonians Cowboy Junkies, especially the sweet organ. The stoic and twangy �Don�t Fault the Stars for Falling� could have been a Dolly Parton tune.
A Grand Expanse
�A Grand Expanse� has a more ambitious arrangement.  It sounds like the end-credits song from a long-ago film we only vaguely remember. It says everything it needs to in one minute and twenty seconds and exactly 38 words. It is quintessential Tiny Sun.
The entire recording feels like music from a dream, and since no one knows exactly what dream music sounds like, this could be it.

items.body: In August 1819, tens of thousands of working men and women gathered in St. Peter�s Field in Manchester to hear the politician Henry Hunt speak. They were difficult times, many still out of work after the Napoleonic wars, rising prices and low wages � and always those at the bottom of the heap suffering. Hunt was a famed orator, a man on the side of the people, able to stir and inspire with his voice. Although the gathering was peaceful, the size of the crowd terrified the magistrates, who panicked and imagined an uprising. They sent in half-trained dragoons and the cavalry, who rode down, slashed and killed without compunction or compassion. In the end, 18 died and up to 700 were wounded. It was a stain on the nation, an outrage; prompting Percy Shelley, one of the poetic giants of the age, to write The Masque of Anarchy , with its famous lines: �Rise like Lions after slumber / in unvanquishable number / She your chains to earth like dew / Which in sleep had fallen on you / Ye are many - they are few.� Peterloo, as people called it, remains one of the seminal events in English working-class history, one that Sean Cooney of the Young 'Uns has revisited for this album of original songs, which is lavishly presented in a book with contemporary letters, political cartoons and illustrations to create a multimedia event. It�s ambitious, no doubt about that, and he�s selected some great talent to help � guitarist Sam Carter, the almost ubiquitous fiddler/singer Eliza Carthy, Ben Nicholls supplying background and texture on various instruments, and the Lancashire industrial ballad singer Jennifer Reid, who doubles as narrator. Peter's Field by Sean Cooney, Eliza Carthy, Sam Carter, Jennifer Reid For a small ensemble, they make a powerful noise. The songs capture the feel of the day; the anticipation and excitement at the summer gathering, the joy that turns to terror and flight as the troops charge, then the bitter, mournful aftermath, voiced some powerful melodies and very well-chosen images. As a writer, Cooney often focuses on the personal in the small tales of people like �Sam Bamford� and �Mary Fildes,� while the three short pieces that comprise �The Monkey Rides The Mare� capture the bluster and arrogance of the soldiers. Peter's Field by Sean Cooney, Eliza Carthy, Sam Carter, Jennifer Reid Cooney is a persuasive singer, and on this heartfelt project, he puts plenty of emotion into his voice. Having two other outstanding vocalists alongside him makes for a wonderful triple threat. In these days when governments across the world are cracking down on protest, this stands as a sobering and very timely reminder. It�s a history lesson, yes, but the detail of the history stays in the book, while the music creates a set of songs that will resonate and remain for a long time. Find the artist online. items.body:
Live at Rockpalast 1999
documents a command performance at the Loreley open-air amphitheater by Malcolm �Mac� Rebennack Jr., aka Dr. John. Rockpalast is a live-music TV show broadcast since 1974 by Westdeutscher Rundfunk (WDR), the archival source for this CD-DVD package, and coincidentally a remarkable cultural institution on its own terms.
Taped at the height of Dr. John�s international popularity, backing the singer-pianist-guitarist are New Orleans stalwarts Bobby Broom (guitar), David Barard (bass), and Herman Ernest (drums), a tight quartet that projects authority and engages the crowd from start to close.
A striking UNESCO-designated World Heritage Site set, the Loreley is a slate pinnacle on a mythic horseshoe bend of the Rhine River, memorializing an enduring German literary legend both tragic and romantic. The setting is thus well-suited for Mac�s mystical spirit and lyrical style. By this stage of his career, he characterized his live show as a Mardi Gras revue with a mix of New Orleans standards and some of his most recognizable compositions.
Hence, he opens with the NOLA classic �Iko, Iko,� a half-sung, half-chanted celebration of community participation in the renowned Mardi Gras second-line street procession. Then comes the in-your-face boast �Qualified,� wherein the singer warns, �I got the power to control / I can see clean through you, blind mole / I want to tell you now, I'm qualified / You know that I'm qualified.�
Any Dr. John fan will recognize �I Walk on Guilded Splinters,� a moody, percussively insistent, foreboding expression of the Night Tripper�s immersion in �funknology� (his term), gris-gris herbology, and hoodoo incantation, punctuated with jungle growls and cries, a loopy, spooky slide whistle, and an extended psych-guitar solo: �Walk thru the fire / Fly thru the smoke / See my enemy / At the end of dey rope.�
Every piece in this well- honed set deserves considertion. Although Dr John lived for many years in Los Angeles and New York, his enduring hometown connection shows in the fond inclusion of his own �Sweet Home New Orleans� and �Goin� Back to New Orleans,� and he nods to a key influence with a funky rendering of Duke Ellington�s �I'm Gonna Go Fishin�.� Among other gems are Mac�s Top�10 hit �Right Place, Wrong Time,� and the instantly recognizable closer, Earl King�s �Big Chief,� another Mardi Gras burner.
Regarding his live performance approach, per the notes, �I always play a little bit of everything. I think that�s what music�s about: a little bit of somethin� old, somethin� in the middle, somethin� new, and somethin� as yet uncreated.�
Dr John's�s longtime fans will welcome this archival gem, which also is a solid introduction for any late comers to the party. Surmounting the barriers of language and culture, the power of
At the Rockpalast
is also evident in the enthusiastic audience response. As he declares, �If you�re gonna get off on somethin� you don�t need to know nothin� about it. Music is a universal language.�

items.body: Kr�ta , the latest release on Norway's Taragot label, features a Swede and two Norwegians playing interpretations of mainly traditional tunes from their respective countries. Fiddler Mats Ed�n has long been involved in Swedish folk music, as a player, composer and teacher, and in the process exploring and integrating different musical styles and approaches. Tellef Kvifte was in the pioneering Norwegian crossover band Slinkombas in the 1970s and has continued to play a central role in Norwegian folk music, both as a musician and an academic. Most often heard playing the sj�fl�yte , more widely known as a recorder, Kvifte has employed other instruments from outside the Norwegian tradition, in particular the saxophone and bagpipes. His son Knut Kvifte Nesheim , a drummer and composer, has also shown a determination to blur the lines between different musical genres, both in his solo and group projects. Kr�ta by Ed�n/Kvifte/Nesheim trio It comes as no surprise then to find this trio offering a far from conventional take on the tunes they have chosen. While dance tunes may be the source of most of the material here, this feels more akin to chamber music; not that it is remotely classical in style, but in the sense it conveys of three players engrossed in a musically intimate conversation. This is not a performance appropriate for accompanying dancers but might instead be seen as an exploration of hidden possibilities of meaning in the music. In so doing it reveals some of its underlying mystery, including, perhaps, a darker side. Just as in an Ibsen play, where the surface bonhomie, jollity and social nicety can be hiding something more sinister, in Scandinavian dance music there are at times hints of a troublesome undercurrent below the surface. So the decision to open proceedings with �Fossgrimen,� a fiddle tune from Norway's Setesdal valley, is perhaps significant. A fossgrimen is a mythical creature, a kind of water-sprite living in waterfalls from whom fiddle-players were considered to have learned their skills and for that were not universally welcomed, with the fiddle considered to be the devil's instrument. Kr�ta by Ed�n/Kvifte/Nesheim trio Tellef Kvifte takes the lead melody on most tracks but on the Swedish �Polska from Per Myhr,� having played a repeated introductory riff on the sj�fl�yte, with Mats Ed�n providing an amorphous textural accompaniment below and Nesheim adding some quiet tinkling, it's Ed�n who introduces the tune on the fiddle with Kvifte proceeding to play in unison. It's a short track and almost as soon as it gets going things start to fragment and everything grind to a halt.
